content:
President Donald Trump traveled to San Antonio, Texas on Wednesday to campaign for Republican Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton. Recently, Trump has repeatedly commented on Paxton's appearance, and the related controversy continues to ferment.

The New York Times revealed on September 30 a leaked recording in which Paxton privately complained that Trump's speech at the Republican midterm election conference in Dallas could drag down his campaign. The remarks brought the issue back into the spotlight.

The President himself has yet to respond to the recording.

Last week, while campaigning in Denton, Texas, Trump described Paxton as "sometimes really troublesome," and questioned whether he was even present (when Paxton was in fact there), before reversing course and calling him "the greatest attorney general in the country."

On the final night of the Republican midterm election conference on September 10, Trump said: "I told him: 'Ken, I don't want to embarrass you, but I disagree with you on so many things... I'm not sure if I like your look, I'm not sure if I like the way you dress, I don't like the way you talk.'"

The previous night, Trump had said: "(Paxton) maybe doesn't dress well enough, maybe doesn't speak perfectly, and maybe he's not the most handsome guy I've ever seen."

In early September, speaking in the Oval Office about Paxton's Democratic opponent James Talarico, Trump said: "We have a guy named Ken Paxton. Some people don't like the way he dresses, some people don't like the way he gives interviews or the way he talks."

With less than five weeks until the November midterms, the Texas Senate race remains tight. According to the latest poll released on October 3 by the New York Times and Siena College, Paxton trails Talarico by six percentage points.

Trump's comments on Paxton's appearance appear to have become a recurring pattern.

Dan Cassino, a political science professor at Fairleigh Dickinson University, told HuffPost that Trump has consistently equated masculine physical traits with strong leadership ability.

Cassino pointed out: "The core issue is that Trump has a very clear set of standards for what a good candidate should be like, what they should look like. The good candidate in his mind is male, tall, handsome, dressed in a way that matches his own ideas. If you don't fit that mold, or if you fall short of that stereotype in any way, Trump will see you as not a qualified candidate."

Trump also frequently comments on his own appearance. Speaking in Nebraska on Monday, Trump claimed that supporters had told him he was in such great shape that he looked more impressive than former Presidents George Washington and Abraham Lincoln.

During his first presidential term in 2016, he once asked the crowd: "I think I have tremendous presidential look. Do I look like a president? I think I look like a president... I'm so handsome, right?"

Cassino believes: "When Trump is endorsing someone or campaigning alongside them, and that person doesn't meet his standard, this mindset becomes a problem. What he's saying (about Paxton) means he sees Paxton as not masculine enough, and therefore doesn't look like a good candidate, or someone who will win."

Why would Trump deliberately say these things to Paxton?

Brandon Rottinghaus, a political science professor at the University of Houston, believes Trump may be preparing for the possibility that Paxton loses.

Rottinghaus pointed out: "In the end, the question is: who's going to take the blame? The President may be setting up a situation so that Paxton will be the one to carry the can for a possible loss in Texas. Trump doesn't want to be the one everyone says caused the Republicans to lose."

However, Rottinghaus emphasized that this is only his personal speculation.

He said: "It's always hard to guess the President's strategy, because on these issues he tends to speak off the cuff. Paxton needs Trump's endorsement and backing, and Trump is happy to treat Paxton as a joke."

Josh Blank, director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin, offers two other interpretations. The first is that these remarks may simply reflect his frustration with the trouble Paxton has caused the Republicans.

Blank told HuffPost: "If the President is over-focusing on Ken Paxton's negative traits, it may just be an expression of frustration."

Another possibility is that these remarks give voters a trivial, harmless flaw to focus on, "so that voters can acknowledge he has shortcomings while at the same time forgiving themselves for continuing to support him."

Throughout Paxton's political career, he has faced allegations including securities fraud, corruption, bribery, abuse of office, and retaliating against whistleblowers. Blank also noted that Paxton has consistently refused to debate Talarico.

Blank said: "This is not a normal election. If Republicans start acting strangely in the final months of the campaign, it's because they're not used to being in this position."

Cal Jillson, a political science professor at Southern Methodist University who specializes in Texas politics, believes Paxton's base will very likely continue to support him.

Speaking about Paxton, Jillson said: "I was chatting with a close friend yesterday, and he said: 'You know what, he's a crook, but he's our crook.' That sums up how the Republican base feels."

Why does this election matter?

Paxton is very well known in Texas. After serving a decade in the state legislature, he was elected attorney general in 2014. He has been a steadfast supporter of the Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement since 2016, and has received millions of dollars in campaign donations through a Texas-based new political action committee linked to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, MAGA Inc., and other Republican groups.

Jillson pointed out that a loss would carry much broader implications. "If Paxton loses, and the gubernatorial race is very, very close, the consequences would be catastrophic."

As of the time of publication, Paxton's team had not responded to HuffPost's request for comment.

Zach Kraft, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, responded to HuffPost's inquiry by saying: "President Trump has called Ken Paxton the strongest attorney general in history, and has made it clear that he will do everything in his power to help him become the next U.S. Senator from Texas. As Texans learn more about James Talarico's radical agenda—eliminating oil and gas, raising taxes, and forcing gender transitions on children—they will realize more and more that they want absolutely nothing to do with this man."
